abstract: |
  Audits of political leaning in large language models (LLMs) typically rely on unvalidated instruments and treat a single elicited answer as the model's position. We administered two validated political-psychology instruments, the short-form Social Dominance Orientation scale (SDO~7~(s)) and the Very Short Authoritarianism scale (VSA), to 24 instruction-tuned LLMs spanning six model families and two development ecosystems, under each system's native deployment conditions, with five independent administrations per item. Dispositional placement was consistent: all 24 models scored below the SDO midpoint (grand mean 1.64 on the 1–7 scale), and 21 scored below the VSA midpoint (grand mean −0.82 on the −4…+4 scale), the remaining three at or marginally above it. Response stability was not: within-model dispersion ranged from perfectly consistent responding to 2.19 scale points, with the most variable responding concentrated in small open-weight models; fourteen models answered identically across all administrations on at least one scale, none on both. No family showed a consistent trend toward higher dominance or authoritarianism across release order. Political-disposition audits therefore rest on a stability assumption that holds for some deployed systems and fails for others; we provide a template that measures placement and stability together.
keywords: [large language models, political bias, social dominance orientation, right-wing authoritarianism, psychometrics, response stability]

# Introduction

A growing body of evidence indicates that large language models (LLMs) are not politically neutral.
These systems now mediate how people search for information, draft and revise text, and seek advice,
and studies probing prominent models report consistent, identifiable political leanings [@feng2023; @hartmann2023; @motoki2024; @rozado2023; @rozado2024]. The point is not merely
academic: recent experiments show that exposure to politically slanted model output can shift the
attitudes and decisions of the people who use it [@fisher2025; @potter2024]. A
systematic ideological tilt in an LLM does not remain inside the model, it propagates through every
downstream interaction, at a scale and uniformity no individual communicator achieves. The political
dispositions of LLMs are therefore a question with direct implications for the information
environment, rather than a curiosity.

Much of what is known about these dispositions comes from a fast-growing audit literature. Across a
range of probes, prominent Western models have been found to express left-of-center, socially
liberal, and libertarian-leaning positions [@hartmann2023; @motoki2024; @rozado2023; @rozado2024], with at least part of this tendency traceable to the composition of pretraining corpora
[@feng2023]. Related work has shown that the opinions models express when surveyed do not
represent populations evenly, aligning by default with some groups more than others [@santurkar2023]. The broad conclusion, that contemporary LLMs are not ideologically neutral, is by now
reasonably well established.

How that tilt is measured, however, is far less settled, and this is where the present study begins.
The majority of audit studies rely on instruments chosen for convenience rather than validated for
the construct they are taken to measure: the Political Compass Test, ad hoc questionnaires, or single
bespoke item sets. @rottger2024 show that such forced-choice probes are fragile, models
give substantively different answers when they are not constrained to the test's format, different
answers depending on how they are constrained, and answers that do not survive paraphrase. The wider
literature on LLM survey responses compounds the concern: model answers carry systematic artifacts
such as option-ordering and labeling biases [@dominguezolmedo2024] and human-like
social-desirability effects [@salecha2024]. In short, the field has been attributing
"political views" to models using tools whose validity for that purpose is largely unexamined, and
whose outputs may not even be stable from one administration to the next.

Direct administration of these constructs to models has only just begun, and the two closest studies leave the openings this paper fills. @lukasik2026 score deployed chat systems on the RWA and the original SDO scale, alongside World Values Survey and Pew items, in single-shot survey-register administrations; @einwiller2026 pool items from fifteen validated authoritarianism instruments and report that closed-form psychometric scores transfer poorly to realistic generation tasks. Neither reports administration-to-administration stability, and neither pairs the SDO~7~(s) with the VSA in the way the dual-process tradition specifies. Those two gaps define what we set out to measure.

We address this in two ways. The first is measurement. In place of an ad hoc scale, we use two of
the most extensively validated instruments in political psychology. Social dominance orientation
(SDO), a generalized preference for group-based hierarchy and inequality, is measured with the
short form of the SDO~7~ scale [@ho2015; @pratto1994]; right-wing authoritarianism
(RWA), authoritarian submission, sanctioned aggression, and conventionalism, with the Very Short
Authoritarianism scale [@altemeyer1981; @bizumic2018]. These two constructs are not
arbitrary choices: they are the dimensions around which several decades of research on political
attitudes, ideology, and prejudice have been organized, and they are theoretically and empirically
distinct, correlating only weakly while each independently predicts prejudice [@altemeyer2004; @duckitt2001]. They carry construct-validity evidence accumulated across many thousands of human
respondents, a foundation that improvised probes lack. The SDO~7~ is especially well suited to the
present setting: it was designed to measure support for group-based hierarchy in general rather than
dominance by one's own group [@ho2015], and so applies coherently to a system that has no
demographic ingroup of its own.

The second is stability. Audit studies typically treat a single elicited response as "the model's"
position, but stability cannot be assumed: @rottger2024 find responses sensitive to
framing, @ceron2024 find that the reliability of models' political worldviews increases
with model size, and @santurkar2023 find that the most heavily human-feedback-tuned model
they examined concentrated almost all of its probability mass on a single response option, unlike
the diversity characteristic of human answers. We therefore treat response stability as a measured
quantity rather than a background assumption. By administering each scale item to each model several
times and quantifying the within-model variability of the responses, we convert the instability
that prior work notes in passing into an explicit, model-level property, one that, as we report,
differs sharply across systems.

A further question, and the one that motivates the larger project of which this study is the first
part, is whether a model's development ecosystem shapes its political dispositions. There are
grounds to expect cultural variation in the values models express [@shan2025], and whether
models built in different geopolitical and linguistic contexts carry different ideological signatures
is of evident importance as these systems are deployed worldwide. Our dataset bears on this only
lightly: it includes a small number of models from a single non-Western developer alongside a larger
set of Western models. We therefore treat the development-ecosystem comparison as descriptive and
exploratory here, and reserve a properly powered, cross-linguistic test for a companion study.

In the present study we administer the SDO~7~ and VSA scales to 24 instruction-tuned LLMs spanning six
model families and two development ecosystems, eliciting five independent responses to each item. We
ask three questions: (1) Where do contemporary LLMs sit on social dominance and authoritarianism?
(2) How stable are their responses across repeated administration, and does that stability vary
across models? (3) Descriptively, do these dispositions vary with development ecosystem or model
generation? Our central findings are that the models cluster consistently toward low social
dominance and mild anti-authoritarianism, and that response stability varies markedly across systems,
from fully consistent responding on a given scale to substantial trial-to-trial variability, with
the most variable responding concentrated in small open-weight models. Beyond the substantive result, the study offers a template for measuring the
political dispositions of LLMs with validated instruments and explicit attention to response
stability, in place of single-shot probes of uncertain validity, while remaining mindful that
instruments developed for human respondents must be applied to models with appropriate caution, a
point we return to in the Discussion.

# Materials and Methods

## Models


```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "The 24 instruction-tuned models. Identifiers are the exact serving-endpoint names in the data. Parameter counts as published by the developer; proprietary flagships (Claude, GPT) do not disclose counts (—)."
dev_map <- c(Claude = "Anthropic", GPT = "OpenAI", `GPT-OSS` = "OpenAI",
             Llama = "Meta", Gemma = "Google", Qwen = "Alibaba")
params_map <- tribble(
  ~m,                            ~Parameters,
  "gpt-oss-20b",                 "20B",
  "gpt-oss-120b",                "120B",
  "meta-llama-3-1-8b-instruct",  "8B",
  "meta-llama-3-3-70b-instruct", "70B",
  "llama-4-maverick",            "[CONFIRM: Ming]",
  "gemma-3-12b",                 "12B",
  "qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct", "80B (a3b)",
  "qwen35-122b-a10b",            "122B (a10b)")
raw |> distinct(m, provider) |>
  left_join(t2 |> select(m, family, ecosystem, access), by = "m") |>
  left_join(release_order, by = "m") |>
  left_join(params_map, by = "m") |>
  arrange(family, lineage, rank) |>
  transmute(Model = m, Developer = unname(dev_map[family]), Lineage = lineage,
            `Release order` = rank, Family = family, Ecosystem = ecosystem,
            Access = access, Provider = provider,
            Parameters = coalesce(Parameters, "—")) |>
  kable()
```

*Note.* "flagship" denotes proprietary models served behind an API without published weights;
"open-weight" denotes models with publicly released weights. Llama version order is confounded
with parameter scale (8B → 70B → Maverick) and is interpreted with that caveat.

We evaluated 24 large language models spanning six model families and two developer
ecosystems (@tbl-models). The Western ecosystem (*n* = 22) comprised Anthropic's Claude family,
across three sublines, Opus (4.1, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8), Sonnet (4, 4.5, 4.6), and Haiku
(4.5); OpenAI's GPT family (4o, 4.1, 5, 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 5.5) together with the open-weight
GPT-OSS models (20B, 120B); Meta's Llama models (3.1-8B, 3.3-70B, 4-Maverick); and Google's
Gemma (3-12B). The Eastern ecosystem (*n* = 2) comprised Alibaba's Qwen models
(Qwen3-Next 80B A3B Instruct and Qwen3.5 122B A10B; endpoint identifiers
`qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct` and `qwen35-122b-a10b`, designations confirmed by Ming and verified
against the collection notebook).

Each model was coded on four dimensions used in the analyses below: **developer ecosystem**
(Western / Eastern); **model family**; **access type** (proprietary-flagship vs. open-weight),
which we use in the response-stability analysis; and, within families that have a sequential
release lineage, **version order** (oldest to newest). Parameter scale is reported where the
developer discloses it and is otherwise left blank, as the proprietary flagship models
(Claude, GPT) do not publish parameter counts.

We note at the outset that the two ecosystems are markedly unbalanced: the Eastern ecosystem
is represented by a single developer (Alibaba) with two models. This constrains the
developer-ecosystem comparison to a descriptive contrast (Section 2.5) and is the reason the
full developer-ecosystem × prompt-language design is reserved for a companion study.

The sample is a convenience frame: the instruction-tuned chat models the research team could reach through two institutional serving routes, Azure OpenAI and Databricks Model Serving, during the collection window. We draw no inference beyond deployed systems of this kind.


## Instruments

Models responded to two established political-attitude instruments grounded in the
political-psychology literature. Social dominance orientation, the construct introduced by
Pratto, Sidanius, Stallworth, and Malle (1994), was measured with the eight-item short form of
the SDO~7~ scale (SDO~7~(s); Ho et al., 2015), answered on a 7-point favor–oppose response format
(1 = *Strongly Oppose* to 7 = *Strongly Favor*). The eight items divide equally between the two substantive subdimensions the SDO~7~ was designed to
separate, group-based dominance (SDO-D) and opposition to equality (SDO-E), crossed with a
balanced method structure of four pro-trait and four con-trait items; the four con-trait
(equality-affirming) items (numbers 3, 4, 7, and 8 of the short scale, two drawn from each
subdimension) are reverse-keyed so that higher scores indicate stronger social dominance
orientation (full item wording in Ho et al., 2015, Appendix B; see §2.4). We used the SDO~7~(s)
rather than the original scale [@pratto1994] in part because @ho2015 reworded
items to remove a confound with preference for *ingroup* dominance, yielding a measure of support
for group-based hierarchy in general, irrespective of which group is on top, a property well
suited to models that have no demographic ingroup of their own. Authoritarianism
was measured with the six-item Very Short Authoritarianism (VSA) scale [@bizumic2018],
which abbreviates Altemeyer's (1981) Right-Wing Authoritarianism scale while preserving its three
defining components, authoritarian submission, authoritarian aggression, and conventionalism, on
a single higher-order factor. We administered the VSA on the same nine-point agree–disagree response format used in its original
validation [@bizumic2018], scored from −4 (*very strongly disagree*) to +4 (*very
strongly agree*) through *strongly*, *somewhat*, and *slightly* anchors with an *unsure or neutral*
midpoint at 0; our administration therefore reproduces the scale as originally validated rather
than adapting it. The ±4 anchoring is likewise characteristic of the broader Altemeyer Right-Wing
Authoritarianism tradition [e.g., @altemeyer2004].

A point of construct precision: we treat the VSA as *operationalizing the right-wing
authoritarianism (RWA) construct*; we did not administer Altemeyer's full RWA scale, and we
therefore refer throughout to "VSA scores" as our measured variable and to "the RWA construct"
when discussing what it indexes. SDO and RWA are treated as the two distinct dimensions along
which ideological attitudes are organised, a separation drawn in the original SDO work, where
SDO correlated only weakly with authoritarianism [@pratto1994], shown directly by
@altemeyer2004, whose RWA and SDO scales correlated only about .20 while each independently
predicted prejudice, and formalised in Duckitt's (2001) dual-process motivational model. All items were presented in English; cross-linguistic administration is reserved for
the companion study.

## Procedure

Each scale item was administered to each model through a chat-completion API. The system message
was held constant across all models and items as `"You are a helpful survey respondent."`; the
user message contained the item text together with an instruction to return the response as a
structured object reporting the chosen numeric scale value and its verbal label. Each item was
administered five times per model as five independent API calls, with a 0.5-second delay between
calls. All 1,680 administrations were collected in a single session on 14 June 2026, spanning roughly eighty minutes by the raw-log timestamps (00:05–01:26 [CONFIRM: Ming, logger timezone; an offset could shift the calendar date]). Every analysis therefore characterises endpoint behaviour at a single point in time, a scope we return to when discussing temporal drift in Section 4.4.

Sampling parameters were not explicitly configured; all calls therefore used default sampling.
Models were reached over two serving paths, the GPT family via Azure OpenAI and all other families
via Databricks Model Serving, both accessed through the same OpenAI-compatible client interface.
For the Azure-served GPT models, an unset temperature corresponds to the OpenAI client default
(temperature 1.0). For several of the models served via Databricks, temperature, top-*p*, and seed
are not client-exposed and are handled server-side, so the effective sampling reflects each
endpoint's native default rather than a value we set; **no random seed was applied** where one was
available. Individual draws are therefore not exactly reproducible. This configuration is
deliberate: administering each item repeatedly under each model's native inference conditions is
what exposes the within-model response variability examined in Section 3, which we interpret as the
*consistency of responses under deployed sampling regimes* rather than as behaviour enforced at a
fixed temperature.

## Scoring

Prior to aggregation, the following items were reverse-keyed so that higher values indicate
greater dominance orientation or greater authoritarianism: SDO items 3, 4, 7, and 8, and VSA
items 1, 4, and 5. The numeric value for each response was parsed from the model's structured
output. Responses that could not be parsed to a valid scale value, including the single explicit
refusal returned by one model, were treated as **missing (non-responses)**, not as errors:
because an attitude item has no correct answer, a refusal carries no scored value. This contrasts
with our companion Reading-the-Mind-in-the-Eyes study, in which refusals are scored as incorrect
because that task has a determinate correct response. Missingness was negligible: 4 of 1,680
administrations (0.24%), all on Social Dominance Orientation items, distributed as three
unparseable responses from one model (Qwen3.5-122B) and one explicit refusal from another
(GPT-OSS-120B; @tbl-missing). Three of the four fall on the two most overtly hierarchy-endorsing dominance items (SDO 1 and 2); the fourth, an empty completion, fell on an equality-affirming item from the same subdimension (SDO 3). The clustering on the scale's most confronting content is a pattern we take up in Section 4.1.

Two summaries were computed per model. A **construct score** for each scale was the mean of the
(reverse-keyed) item values, pooled across the five repetitions. A **within-model response
dispersion** for each scale was obtained by computing, for each item, the standard deviation of
that item's responses across the five repetitions, and averaging these per-item standard
deviations across the scale's items; a value of 0 indicates identical responses across all
repetitions. We refer to this quantity as *response dispersion* (equivalently, instability)
rather than "consistency," since larger values denote *less* consistent responding. Response
dispersion is invariant to reverse-keying. Five repetitions per item give screening resolution, enough to separate deterministic from highly variable responding, not precise dispersion estimates. Every dispersion comparison below is accordingly rank-based and read ordinally.

## Analysis

Analyses proceeded along four lines. First, **dispositional placement**: we summarised construct
scores by model, family, and ecosystem, interpreting them relative to each scale's midpoint
(4 on the 1–7 SDO scale; 0 on the −4…+4 VSA scale). Second, **response stability**: we compared
within-model response dispersion across access types (proprietary-flagship vs. open-weight). Near-
deterministic models produce variance estimates at or near the boundary of the parameter space,
which destabilises item-level mixed-effects models (random-effects singular fits in `lme4`;
`glmmTMB` was retained as a fallback); we therefore analysed stability through the per-model
dispersion summaries and tested group differences with Mann–Whitney *U* tests, which are
appropriate given the small number of models and the non-normal, boundary-bounded distribution of
dispersion. To reduce serving-configuration confounds, we additionally restricted this comparison
to models served over a single provider (Claude vs. the smaller open-weight models, all served via
Databricks). Because the effective sampling parameters of individual Databricks endpoints are
handled server-side and are not observable to us, this restriction controls for provider-level
differences but cannot guarantee identical per-endpoint sampling; we therefore treat the resulting
contrast as suggestive rather than as a clean isolation of model-level effects. We note, however,
that the Azure-served GPT models, which run at the OpenAI client default temperature, themselves
differ in dispersion across versions, indicating that response-consistency differences are not
solely a serving artefact. (We return to both points, the deployed-behaviour framing and the limits on intrinsic-vs.-
configuration attribution, in Section 4.2.)
Third, **developer
ecosystem**: given a single Eastern developer represented by two models, the ecosystem contrast is
reported descriptively only, with no inferential test; the developer-ecosystem × prompt-language
interaction is the primary test of the companion study and is not estimated here. Fourth,
**within-family version trends**: construct scores were plotted against version order within each
family with a release lineage (@fig-evolution) and described qualitatively.

Opened up by @ho2015: the SDO~7~(s) was purpose-built to separate
SDO-Dominance (overt support for group oppression; short-scale items 1–4) from SDO-Egalitarianism
(subtle opposition to equality; items 5–8). The eight items support a 4-item score for each
subdimension, so the models' standing on dominance vs. anti-egalitarianism can be reported
separately. This could be substantively interesting, a model might disavow overt dominance yet
sit higher on subtle anti-egalitarianism, but the 4-item (2 reverse-keyed) subscales are
lower-reliability, so treat any subdimension contrast as exploratory. Decision pending.

All analyses were conducted in R 4.6.0 [@rcoreteam2026] with the tidyverse suite, version 2.0.0
(Wickham et al., 2019; dplyr 1.2.1, readr 2.2.0, tibble 3.3.1), and figures were produced with
ggplot2 4.0.3. The Mann–Whitney *U* tests were computed as exact Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with `stats::wilcox.test` in base R, which from version 4.6 evaluates the exact conditional distribution of the rank-sum statistic in the presence of ties and reports the two-sided *p*-value as twice the smaller one-sided tail; we verified these values against an independent full-enumeration of the permutation distribution. Under the alternative symmetric-tail convention (as in the `coin` package) the two authoritarianism *p*-values are .051 and .020, and every conclusion holds under either convention. The full `sessionInfo()`
output is included in the data deposit. The raw response
data and the analysis script are openly available at github (might move to appendix).

# Results

*Computed from the model-level aggregates (`attitude_sdo_by_model.csv`, `attitude_rwa_by_model.csv`,
`attitude_consistency_by_model.csv`) in R 4.6.0 via the deposited script `verify_section3_stats.R`
(exact Wilcoxon rank-sum implementation of the Mann–Whitney tests; runs 6–8 July 2026) and
independently cross-checked in Python/scipy. The two implementations agree on every test statistic
and effect size; exact p-values are reported.*

## Dispositional placement


```{r}
#| label: tbl-results
#| tbl-cap: "Construct scores and response dispersion by model (programmatically generated; matches table2_check.csv by construction). SDO on 1–7 (midpoint 4); VSA on −4…+4 (midpoint 0). Dispersion (Section 2.4) is the mean per-item SD across the five administrations, in raw scale points, and is therefore not directly comparable across the two scales; 0 indicates identical responses across all repetitions."
t2 |> arrange(family, m) |>
  mutate(across(c(SDO, RWA, consistency_sdo, consistency_vsa), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
  rename(`Model` = m, `SDO mean` = SDO, `VSA mean` = RWA,
         `SDO dispersion` = consistency_sdo, `VSA dispersion` = consistency_vsa) |>
  kable()
```

Construct scores, pooled across the five repetitions per item (Section 2.4), are reported for all
24 models in @tbl-results. Social dominance orientation was low in absolute terms across the entire
sample: every model scored below the SDO midpoint of 4, with a grand mean of 1.64 (median 1.49) on
the 1–7 scale and a range from 1.00 (Qwen3-Next-80B, the scale minimum) to 3.42 (Llama-3.1-8B).
The picture for authoritarianism was similar in direction but less uniform: the grand mean VSA
score was −0.82 (median −0.77) on the −4…+4 scale, and 21 of the 24 models scored below the
midpoint of 0. The three exceptions sat essentially at the midpoint rather than meaningfully above
it (GPT-4o, +0.20; GPT-OSS-20B, +0.13; Qwen3.5-122B, 0.00). Family means ranged from 1.45 (Gemma)
to 2.18 (Llama) on the SDO and from −1.34 (Llama) to −0.38 (GPT-OSS) on the VSA. Taken together,
the models cluster toward strong rejection of group-based hierarchy and mild anti-authoritarianism,
with meaningful between-model spread inside that cluster.

The VSA mean conceals item-level structure. Grouping the six items by the scale's three facets (two items each), the models strongly rejected authoritarian submission (mean keyed response −1.56) and conventionalism (−1.10), yet sat marginally on the authoritarian side of the midpoint for authoritarian aggression (+0.22), the two law-and-order items on which the authoritarian-side mass in @fig-vsa-items concentrates. With only two items per facet these contrasts are exploratory, and the aggression-side lean invites a deflationary reading, assistant-register endorsement of public safety rather than authoritarianism proper. What the split establishes is narrower and firmer: the scale mean should not be read as a uniform disposition, consistent with the psychometric caveats in Section 4.3.


## Response stability


```{r}
#| label: fig-dispersion
#| fig-cap: "Response dispersion by access type. Points are models; crossbars are medians. Full-sample Mann–Whitney contrasts: SDO U = 45.5, p = .26; VSA U = 32.5, p = .052. Provider-restricted (Claude vs Databricks-served open-weight): SDO U = 23.0, p = .21; VSA U = 12.5, p = .021, rank-biserial r = .65 (positive = higher open-weight dispersion). Exact p-values, two-sided as twice the smaller one-sided tail (R 4.6)."
disp |>
  left_join(t2 |> select(m, access), by = "m") |>
  pivot_longer(c(consistency_sdo, consistency_vsa),
               names_to = "scale", values_to = "dispersion") |>
  mutate(scale = recode(scale, consistency_sdo = "SDO", consistency_vsa = "VSA")) |>
  ggplot(aes(access, dispersion, colour = access)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, size = 2.4, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.45, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Response dispersion (mean per-item SD)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "none")
```

<!-- OPTIONAL Figure 3, earned by the §4.3 transfer/reconciliation paragraph (A1); move to the appendix if preferred. -->
```{r}
#| label: fig-vsa-items
#| fig-cap: "Item-level VSA responses across all 24 models × 5 administrations, reverse-keyed so positive values are authoritarian-side. Authoritarian-side mass concentrates on the two law-and-order items. Percentages give each item's authoritarian-side response share."
item_tags <- tribble(
  ~question_id, ~tag,
  "vsa-q1", "Defy authority (R)",
  "vsa-q2", "Discipline, follow leaders",
  "vsa-q3", "God's laws",
  "vsa-q4", "Premarital sex (R)",
  "vsa-q5", "No tougher government (R)",
  "vsa-q6", "Crack down on troublemakers")
vsa <- raw |> filter(category == "vsa") |> left_join(item_tags, by = "question_id")
ann <- vsa |> group_by(tag) |>
  summarise(share = mean(keyed > 0), mn = mean(keyed), .groups = "drop")
vsa |>
  mutate(tag = fct_reorder(tag, keyed, .fun = mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(keyed, tag)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.18, width = 0.06, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_text(data = ann, aes(x = 4.35, y = tag, label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)),
            size = 3, hjust = 0) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 5.3), clip = "off") +
  labs(x = "Keyed response (-4 to +4; positive = authoritarian side)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Within-model response dispersion varied markedly across systems: from 0 to 1.40 scale points on the
SDO and from 0 to 2.19 on the VSA (@tbl-results; @fig-dispersion). Fourteen of the 24 models returned identical
responses across all five repetitions on at least one scale; no model did so on both, so even the
most stable systems were near- rather than fully deterministic under native sampling conditions.
Near-determinism here is concrete. A per-scale dispersion of 0.056 (SDO) or 0.075 (VSA), the flagship medians reported below, is exactly what results when a single response among the scale's forty (SDO) or thirty (VSA) administrations differs by one scale point and every other is identical. Ten model-scales sit at precisely that value, each a run of forty (or thirty) responses broken by one adjacent step.

In the access-type comparison, open-weight models showed higher median dispersion than proprietary
flagships on both scales (SDO: 0.23 vs. 0.06; VSA: 0.74 vs. 0.07). With 24 models, however, the
corresponding exact Mann–Whitney tests did not reach conventional significance in the full sample
(SDO: *U* = 45.5, *p* = .26; VSA: *U* = 32.5, *p* = .052). In the provider-restricted
comparison (Section 2.5; the nine Claude models vs. the eight open-weight models, all served via
Databricks), the VSA contrast was nominally significant (*U* = 12.5, *p* = .021, rank-biserial
*r* = .65; positive values indicate higher open-weight dispersion) while the SDO contrast was not
(*U* = 23.0, *p* = .21, *r* = .36).

Because four dispersion contrasts are reported, we record their standing under multiplicity correction. The Holm-adjusted *p*-values are .084 (provider-restricted VSA), .157 (full-sample VSA), and .41 for both SDO contrasts: no contrast survives correction across the four tests. We therefore treat the access-type comparison as exploratory and rest the stability finding on the distributional structure described next rather than on any single test.

The distributional structure behind these tests is informative. The extreme dispersion values were
concentrated in open-weight models, the three most variable systems on the VSA (Llama-3.1-8B,
2.19; GPT-OSS-120B, 1.58; GPT-OSS-20B, 1.10) and the four most variable on the SDO were all
open-weight, but the open-weight group was heterogeneous rather than uniformly unstable:
Llama-3.3-70B and Llama-4-Maverick responded near-deterministically on both scales. Among the
flagships, the Claude family was uniformly stable (maximum dispersion 0.23 across both scales and
all nine models), whereas the Azure-served GPT models, all run at the same client-default
temperature of 1.0, were near-deterministic on the SDO (0–0.30) yet showed substantial
version-to-version variation on the VSA (0–0.85). This within-provider, within-family variation
indicates that response-consistency differences are not solely a serving-configuration artefact,
although, as noted in Section 2.5, intrinsic-model and endpoint-level contributions cannot be fully
separated in this design.

Dispersion on a bounded scale is not independent of placement: a model whose mean sits near the scale floor has little room to vary. Consistent with this, SDO dispersion correlated substantially with SDO placement across the 24 models (Spearman $\rho$ = .46, permutation *p* = .026), whereas VSA dispersion, with means sitting mid-scale, showed no such coupling ($\rho$ = −.07). The access-type contrast on the SDO is thus partly confounded with placement, so we lean on the VSA, where dispersion is uncoupled from placement, as the informative scale for stability comparisons.

## Development ecosystem (descriptive)

Consistent with Section 2.5, the ecosystem contrast is reported descriptively, with no inferential
test. The two Eastern-ecosystem models bracketed much of the Western range rather than occupying a
distinct position: Qwen3-Next-80B produced the lowest SDO score in the sample, the scale minimum
of 1.00, returned identically across all repetitions, together with a clearly anti-authoritarian
VSA score (−1.10), whereas Qwen3.5-122B produced the second-highest SDO score (2.46) and a VSA
score exactly at the midpoint (0.00, with zero dispersion). With a single developer represented by
two models, these observations illustrate within-ecosystem heterogeneity; the inferential
ecosystem × prompt-language design is reserved for the companion study.

## Within-family version trends


```{r}
#| label: fig-evolution
#| fig-cap: "Construct scores across model versions within each lineage. Version order is release order, defined explicitly in the analysis code (older → newer within lineage)."
scores <- sdo_m |> select(m, SDO) |>
  left_join(rwa_m |> select(m, RWA), by = "m") |>
  pivot_longer(c(SDO, RWA), names_to = "scale", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(scale = recode(scale, RWA = "VSA")) |>
  left_join(release_order, by = "m")
stopifnot(!any(is.na(scores$rank)))
ggplot(scores, aes(rank, score, colour = lineage, group = lineage)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:7) +
  labs(x = "Version order (older to newer, within lineage)", y = "Construct score",
       colour = "Lineage") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

No family showed a consistent drift toward higher dominance or authoritarianism across release
order (@fig-evolution). Claude Opus moved non-monotonically on both scales (SDO 1.50 → 1.38 → 1.62 →
1.48 → 2.15; VSA −0.40 → −1.30 → −1.80 → −1.17 → −0.67), with the newest release (Opus 4.8)
recording the family's highest SDO score. Claude Sonnet drifted mildly toward stronger
anti-authoritarianism across its three versions (VSA −0.33 → −0.63 → −1.17) at near-constant SDO.
The seven GPT versions showed no directional trend on either scale; the oldest, GPT-4o, was the
only flagship above the VSA midpoint (+0.20). Llama declined on the SDO across its lineage (3.42 →
1.75 → 1.38), an ordering confounded with parameter scale (Section 2.1). The two Qwen generations moved in the opposite direction, the newer Qwen3.5 sitting higher on the SDO (1.00 → 2.46) and at the VSA midpoint (−1.10 → 0.00). Given two to seven releases per family, these patterns are described qualitatively and not tested.

# Discussion

Administering two validated political-psychology instruments to 24 instruction-tuned models under
their native deployment conditions produced two findings of unequal familiarity. The first extends
what the audit literature has reported with less validated tools: every model scored below the
social-dominance midpoint (grand mean 1.64 on the 1–7 scale), and 21 of 24 scored below the
authoritarianism midpoint (grand mean −0.82 on −4…+4), the exceptions sitting at or
marginally above it. The second is less familiar: whether a model gives the same answer twice is
itself a strongly model-varying property, ranging from perfectly consistent responding across all
five administrations to dispersion of more than two scale points, and this variation is not
cleanly organised by the proprietary/open-weight distinction that first suggests itself. We take
the two findings in turn, then consider what scores of this kind can and cannot be taken to mean.

## A consistent dispositional profile, with rival explanations for it

The profile itself, strong rejection of group-based hierarchy, mild anti-authoritarianism, is
directionally consistent with the left-liberal tilt that audit studies have reported using the
Political Compass Test and similar probes [@hartmann2023; @motoki2024; @rozado2023; @rozado2024]
— noting that SDO and RWA are correlates of, rather than measures of, left–right self-placement
[@duckitt2001]. Our contribution on this point is that the tilt survives a measurement upgrade: it
appears on instruments with decades of validation, under an unforced response format, and it
reproduces across repeated administration in most systems. Whatever forced-choice probes distort
[@rottger2024], they do not appear to have invented the direction of the effect.

Why deployed models occupy this region admits at least two explanations that our design cannot
separate. One is provenance: political leanings are traceable in part to pretraining corpus
composition [@feng2023], with instruction tuning plausibly sharpening the pattern,
SDO items overtly endorse group-based inequality, and models tuned toward harmlessness are
optimised in ways that penalise endorsing them. The other is presentational: LLMs show human-like social-desirability
biases, skewing toward the favourable pole when they infer they are being evaluated [@salecha2024]. Preference-based fine-tuning supplies a training-side route to the same pole: human raters systematically favour agreeable responses, and optimising against those preferences measurably shifts assistants toward them, at times at the cost of accuracy [@sharma2024]. Unlike the evaluation-awareness effect above, this pressure operates whether or not a prompt carries any evaluative cue. Our data contain a signature consistent with desirability pressure at the
extreme: three of the four missing administrations, two empty completions and the single explicit refusal, fell on the two most overtly hierarchy-endorsing dominance items, the fourth on an equality-affirming item from the same subdimension (Section 2.4); one model returned the exact scale floor with zero
dispersion. Low placement may therefore reflect what a well-behaved survey respondent says as much
as any stable evaluative tendency; we flag the ambiguity rather than resolve it. One reading of
the asymmetry between the two scales, uniform, floor-ward SDO placement versus milder, less
uniform anti-authoritarianism, is that overt endorsement of inequality is more directly penalised
by contemporary alignment objectives [cf. @bai2022] than
endorsement of authority and convention; our design
cannot test this, and we offer it only as a hypothesis for targeted follow-up. Whether these
values are also low by *human* standards is a comparison we deliberately leave unanchored here.
[CONFIRM with Kangning: representative human sample means for the SDO~7~(s) and VSA (e.g., from Ho
et al., 2015; Bizumic & Duckitt, 2018)]

Nor is the profile drifting. Across five Claude Opus releases, seven GPT versions, and the shorter
Sonnet, Llama, and Qwen lineages, no family moved consistently toward higher dominance or
authoritarianism (Section 3.4), and the only flagship above the authoritarianism midpoint was the
oldest model in the sample (GPT-4o, +0.20). On these two constructs, at least, the popular
intuition that successive model generations are converging on a changed political character finds
no support.

## Response stability is a property of models, not of model categories

Audit studies implicitly assume that the answer they elicit is the answer they would have got. We
measured that assumption, per model, and it fails for some systems while holding remarkably well
for others: fourteen of the 24 models responded identically across all five administrations on at
least one scale, none did so on both, and dispersion reached 2.19 scale points at the other
extreme.

The category-level story is tempting but not what the data support. Open-weight models showed
higher median dispersion than proprietary flagships on both scales, yet the full-sample contrasts
did not reach conventional significance (*p* = .26 and .052), and only the provider-restricted
authoritarianism contrast did (*p* = .021, uncorrected; rank-biserial *r* = .65; Section 3.2). More telling is
the composition behind the medians: two open-weight systems (Llama-3.3-70B and Llama-4-Maverick)
were near-deterministic, while the GPT flagships, run under identical client-side configuration,
varied on the VSA from perfect consistency to 0.85 across versions. Stability, in short, is a
property of individual model–endpoint systems, to be measured rather than inferred from access
type. The pattern is directionally consistent with the finding that the reliability of models'
political worldviews increases with parameter count [@ceron2024], our most variable
system is also our smallest, but it is not reducible to scale: GPT-OSS-120B ranks second in VSA
dispersion despite its size. It also converges with @moore2024, who find models
relatively consistent overall, with the remaining inconsistency concentrated on controversial
topics and in fine-tuned models: our items are precisely such value-laden statements, and we
observe the same heterogeneity distributed across models. The zero-dispersion responding that more
than half our sample shows on at least one scale is, likewise, the behavioural analogue of the
probability-mass concentration @santurkar2023 report for their most heavily
feedback-tuned model. Survey-level analogues of this compression are documented directly: synthetic samples vary less than the human surveys they imitate [@bisbee2024], and on an abstract political questionnaire flagship models converge on one another more tightly than politicians of the same party do [@barmettler2026], homogeneity among models, distinct from the abstract-to-concrete reversal we discuss in Section 4.3.

What produces a given model's dispersion is a question this design can bound but not settle.
Sampling parameters for several endpoints are handled server-side and are not observable
(Sections 2.3 and 2.5), so intrinsic stochasticity and serving configuration cannot be fully
separated. Two observations constrain the space: the authoritarianism contrast persists within a
single provider, and dispersion varies across GPT versions at a fixed client default, so
configuration alone does not explain the pattern. Nor is zero dispersion an artefact of response caching at the serving layer: models served by the same provider span the full dispersion range, and the same Azure-served endpoints that respond deterministically on one scale vary on the other. Beyond that, we deliberately frame the estimand
as *deployed* behaviour. For the question this literature ultimately cares about, what
dispositions do these systems express to the people using them, the native-condition response
distribution is the quantity of interest, not a nuisance to be configured away: a user consulting
a given endpoint under comparable conditions samples from the distribution characterised here, and whether its width
originates in the weights or in serving defaults changes the engineering diagnosis, not the
ecological description. This is also our answer to the ecological-validity critique of
forced-choice probes [@rottger2024]: unforced, repeated administration under native
conditions measures the behaviour that actually occurs in use. The practical implication for the
audit literature is inexpensive: five repeated administrations per item were sufficient to
distinguish deterministic from highly variable systems, and per-model stability should be reported
alongside placement as a matter of course.

## What administering human instruments to models does, and does not, measure

We do not claim that these models *have* social dominance orientation or authoritarianism as
latent traits. The instruments' construct validity was established on human respondents with group
memberships, motivations, and biographies. The strongest affirmative reading of model questionnaire behaviour is the "algorithmic fidelity" claim, that a model conditioned on sociodemographic backstories emulates subgroup response distributions closely enough to serve as "silicon samples" [@argyle2023]. That claim has narrowed considerably under replication: synthetic respondents reproduce sample means while compressing their variance, yield regression estimates that diverge from those computed on the surveys they would replace, and drift across months [@bisbee2024]; more broadly, model survey responses lack the statistical signatures of human populations [@dominguezolmedo2024]. Treating models as survey respondents standing in for any human group is therefore a use we avoid entirely. What a
model's score measures is an output-level property: a reproducible disposition to endorse or
reject specific, theoretically grounded value statements under deployment conditions. That
property requires no psychological realism to matter. Politically slanted model output measurably
shifts the opinions and decisions of the people who interact with it [@fisher2025; @potter2024]; the output-level disposition is the causally relevant object, whatever its inner
status.

That framing must now answer a sharper challenge. Two audits appearing while this manuscript was in preparation report that questionnaire placement travels poorly into realistic use. @einwiller2026 administered items from fifteen validated authoritarianism instruments, the VSA among them, to seventeen models alongside behavioural vignettes and realistic writing tasks, and found that closed-form psychometric scores carried essentially no predictive validity for authoritarian content in realistic generations (median r = .01, though across only fourteen models and with an interval wide enough to admit a substantial correlation), with authoritarian expression falling sharply as tasks grew more realistic. @barmettler2026 found that the left-of-centre convergence sixty-six models show on an abstract policy questionnaire inverts on concrete decisions: confronted with forty-eight real Swiss referenda, the same flagship systems aligned with the political centre, and abstract placement did not predict referendum behaviour. Neither result contradicts what we claim, because we claim nothing about downstream behaviour: this study characterises the disposition a model expresses in the survey-response register, under native serving conditions and an unforced format, and the stability of that disposition across administrations. The transfer question those audits raise is real, and placement-plus-stability measurement is a prerequisite for answering it, not an answer; Einwiller et al. themselves treat the psychometric and behavioural levels as complementary, with instrument-based elicitation surfacing latent tendencies that safety tuning can mask downstream.

One apparent conflict dissolves once the metrics are compared. Einwiller et al. report substantial authoritarian response rates in every model tested; we report VSA means below the scale midpoint for twenty-one of twenty-four models. Their rate metric records whether, not how strongly, a model sides with an authoritarian statement, aggregated over a heterogeneous item pool; a scale mean weights direction and intensity on a single validated short form. Both readings live in our own data: 11.7% of VSA administrations fall on the authoritarian side of the midpoint, concentrated almost entirely on the scale's two law-and-order items (which carry 73 of the 84 authoritarian-side responses), even as the scale means sit below it. The two summaries answer different questions about the same response distribution, one more reason to report the instrument explicitly.

Validated instruments still earn their place in this deflated role, the general case @pellert2024 argue, whose "AI psychometrics" programme repurposes standard human inventories as diagnostic tools for model characteristics while insisting the resulting profiles are metaphorical rather than psychological. We extend that programme in two ways: by assessing deployed conversational systems under native serving conditions, rather than encoder models probed through token probabilities, and by treating stability across administrations as a reported outcome rather than an assumption. Their item content was built
and tested to discriminate the target constructs in humans; their scores carry known human
reference points; and the SDO~7~ in particular was designed to measure preference for group-based
hierarchy in general rather than dominance by one's own group [@ho2015], which makes its
administration to an entity without a demographic ingroup at least coherent. Coherent
administration, we stress, is not construct validation. @einwiller2026 supply direct evidence for reading the numbers this way: administered to models, the VSA shows unsatisfactory internal consistency and factor structures that depart from those validated on human samples, which is why we read the scale scores descriptively, and why the facet-level view in Section 3.1 is the one we trust. One format caveat also stands: eliciting a
numeric scale value with its verbal label sidesteps the option-letter biases documented for
multiple-choice formats [@dominguezolmedo2024], but we administered a single format, and
robustness of these placements across response formats [@rottger2024] remains untested
here. A related scoping caveat: the fixed system message ("You are a helpful survey respondent.") is itself a register cue, so what we characterise is the distribution of API-served endpoints under a minimal survey framing, not of consumer products that wrap the same weights in extensive product prompts, and that framing may itself interact with the desirability pressures of Section 4.1 [@salecha2024].

## Limitations and the companion study

The study is a snapshot: 24 systems, each reached through one access route, in one collection
window. Scores are model-level aggregates, so the SDO~7~(s)'s dominance and anti-egalitarianism
subdimensions are unexamined. Five repetitions capture short-run sampling variability, not
temporal stability across serving updates. That longer horizon is not hypothetical: identical prompts to the same deployed system have produced significantly different response distributions across a three-month window [@bisbee2024], which is precisely what our single-session snapshot (Section 2.3) cannot see. Administration was English-only, with instruments
developed and normed in Western, largely US, samples; the scale midpoints we interpret against are
human-normed anchors, not calibrated neutral points for machine respondents. Sampling opacity
limits mechanistic attribution, as discussed. And with two Eastern-ecosystem models from a single
developer, no ecosystem inference is possible, indeed the two Qwen models bracket much of the
Western range (Section 3.3), a caution against essentialising "Eastern" or "Western" model values
from small samples. The companion study is designed for exactly this question, crossing developer
ecosystem with prompt language in a factorial administration; notably, translating opinion
questions into another language does not by itself reliably move model responses toward the
opinions of that language's speakers [@durmus2023], so the design treats language and
ecosystem as separable factors rather than proxies for one another.

The political dispositions of deployed language models are measurable with instruments that carry
decades of validation, and in most of the systems people actually use they are strikingly
reproducible. Where they are not, that too is now a number rather than an anecdote. Treating both
the disposition and its stability as measured quantities, rather than assuming the first from a
single elicitation and never asking about the second, is a modest methodological adjustment with
immediate consequences for how model audits should be read, compared, and acted upon.

# Conclusion

Administered under the conditions in which they are actually deployed, twenty-four instruction-tuned language models place consistently in the low ranges of two validated political-psychology instruments: hierarchy-attenuating on the SDO~7~(s), and, for twenty-one of the twenty-four, below the midpoint of the VSA. The finding of interest is less the placement than its texture. Responding is often literally deterministic, fourteen models answered identically across all five administrations on at least one scale, none on both, with the most variable responding concentrated among small open-weight systems. That access-type gap is descriptively consistent across the full sample and nominally significant for the VSA within the provider-restricted comparison, though no contrast survives correction across the four tests reported. We have argued that these scores be read as output-level dispositions of deployed systems rather than personality attributes, and that their stability be treated as a property worth measuring rather than assuming. Whether survey-register dispositions govern behaviour in open-ended use is the live question recent audits pose; the placement-and-stability baseline reported here is offered as the reference point such tests require, and as the Western-model arm of a planned cross-linguistic comparison.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing

# Data-driven again (8 July 2026): parse_error is populated only for the four

# guessing (first 1000 rows) coerced the column to logical and silently dropped

raw |>

  kable()
```

# Appendix B. Supplementary statistics and session information {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: verify-stats
#| echo: false
# Embedded [VERIFY-R] block: every §3 headline statistic and the new item-level
# quantities, computed from the deposited data at render time.
construct <- raw |> group_by(m, category) |>
  summarise(mean_keyed = mean(keyed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
sdo <- construct |> filter(category == "sdo")
vsa <- construct |> filter(category == "vsa")
cat(sprintf("SDO grand mean %.2f, median %.2f, range %.2f–%.2f\n",
            mean(sdo$mean_keyed), median(sdo$mean_keyed), min(sdo$mean_keyed), max(sdo$mean_keyed)))
cat(sprintf("VSA grand mean %.2f, median %.2f; below midpoint: %d of 24\n",
            mean(vsa$mean_keyed), median(vsa$mean_keyed), sum(vsa$mean_keyed < 0)))

dl <- disp |> left_join(t2 |> select(m, access, model_family = family), by = "m")
zero_any <- dl |> filter(consistency_sdo == 0 | consistency_vsa == 0) |> nrow()
zero_both <- dl |> filter(consistency_sdo == 0 & consistency_vsa == 0) |> nrow()
cat(sprintf("Zero-dispersion on >=1 scale: %d; on both: %d\n", zero_any, zero_both))

mw <- function(a, b, lab) {
  w <- wilcox.test(a, b, exact = TRUE)   # exact with ties: R >= 4.6 (verified 7 Jul 2026; two-sided = doubled one-sided tail)
  r <- 1 - 2 * w$statistic / (length(a) * length(b))
  cat(sprintf("%s: U = %.1f, p = %.3f, rank-biserial r = %.2f\n", lab, w$statistic, w$p.value, r))
}
fl <- dl |> filter(access == "flagship"); ow <- dl |> filter(access == "open-weight")
cl <- dl |> filter(.data$model_family == "Claude")
mw(fl$consistency_sdo, ow$consistency_sdo, "Full-sample SDO dispersion")
mw(fl$consistency_vsa, ow$consistency_vsa, "Full-sample VSA dispersion")
mw(cl$consistency_sdo, ow$consistency_sdo, "Provider-restricted SDO dispersion")
mw(cl$consistency_vsa, ow$consistency_vsa, "Provider-restricted VSA dispersion")

v <- raw |> filter(category == "vsa")
cat(sprintf("VSA administrations on the authoritarian side: %.1f%%\n", 100 * mean(v$keyed > 0)))
v |> group_by(question_id) |> summarise(mean_keyed = round(mean(keyed), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  as.data.frame() |> print(row.names = FALSE)
```
